documents.abstract: While replicability of findings is a cornerstones of empirical research, in various fields adjacent to occupational health, research has shown to be insufficiently reproducible. A discussion on the topic of replicability and questionable research practices is, as far as we are aware, lacking in the field of occupational health. In the current study we therefore aim to evaluate indications of publication bias in the occupational health research literature. Ideally this would be done by large scale replications, which require considerable resources. A less resource-intense alternative is to screen a published body of evidence for indicators of publication bias, which might indicate low replicability and insufficient robustness of the evidence base. In the current protocol, we propose the methods of conducting a z-curve analysis by applying an existing text mining algorithm to articles published in the ten highest ranked occupational health journals. This algorithm can ‘scrape’ abstracts of all publications and extract relevant statistics from it (i.e., p-values and/or confidence intervals of various effect measures). Our pilot data analysis, using data from the years 2010 and 2020 only, was successful as a result of which we expect to be able to carry out the main analyses on the full dataset.

documents.abstract: Human brain and behavior provide a rich venue that can inspire novel control and learning methods for robotics. In an attempt to exemplify such a development by inspiring how humans acquire knowledge and transfer skills among tasks, we introduce a novel multi-task reinforcement learning framework named Episodic Return Progress with Bidirectional Progressive Neural Networks (ERP-BPNN). The proposed ERP-BPNN model 1) learns in a human-like interleaved manner by 2) autonomous task switching based on a novel intrinsic motivation signal and, in contrast to existing methods, 3) allows bidirectional skill transfer among tasks. ERP-BPNN is a general architecture applicable to several multi-task learning settings; in this paper, we present the details of its neural architecture and show its ability to enable effective learning and skill transfer among morphologically different robots in a reaching task. The developed Bidirectional Progressive Neural Network (BPNN) architecture enables bidirectional skill transfer without requiring incremental training and seamlessly integrates with online task arbitration. The task arbitration mechanism developed is based on soft Episodic Return progress (ERP), a novel intrinsic motivation (IM) signal. To evaluate our method, we use quantifiable robotics metrics such as ‘expected distance to goal’ and ‘path straightness’ in addition to the usual reward-based measure of episodic return common in reinforcement learning. With simulation experiments, we show that ERP-BPNN achieves faster cumulative convergence and improves performance in all metrics considered among morphologically different robots compared to the baselines. Overall, our method provides a human-inspired and efficient multi-task reinforcement learning approach with interleaved learning, making it highly suitable for lifelong learning applications.

documents.abstract: Theoretical Background: In the modern world career guidance and counseling is an important tool for an effective functioning of social system, as well as for ensuring the subjective well-being of individual members of society. Due to this fact the scientific interest towards career counseling constantly increases (Garriott et al., 2017). The attention mostly focuses on state policies in the field of career counseling (Kettunen et al., 2016), personality-oriented and value-oriented approaches in counseling (Niles & Guttierez, 2019), possibilities of using computer-assisted career guidance systems (Osborn, 2021), etc. Among other areas of practical implementation, сareer guidance and counseling in the education system is of particular importance. School age, especially adolescence, marks a pivotal stage when individuals face their first career decisions (Sharma, 2022), often without the life experience necessary to fully evaluate their strengths and potential (Marciniak et al., 2020). This period, defined by the development of personal identity, adds complexity to the process of choosing a career (Branje, 2022). External influences, such as parental expectations and peer pressure, can push adolescents toward professions that may not align with their true passions and aspirations (Kazi & Akhlaq, 2017). Additionally, the rapid pace of technological advancement and the emergence of new professions create uncertainty, making it challenging to anticipate future career demands and opportunities (Bankins et al., 2024). However, access to comprehensive career counselling and the cultivation of intrinsic motivation – rooted in personal interests and values – are essential for fostering a well-informed and successful career trajectory as well as for subjective well-being. An important factor in career decision-making activities is career motivation (Guay, 2005; Priyashantha et al., 2022). Within the framework of our study, the theory of Autonomous Career Motivation (ACM) should be considered. ACM is a recently developed construct based on Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000) and related to personal motivation for professional development and career building (Sverko & Babarovic, 2024). Researching the features of autonomous career motivation of Ukrainian high school seniors and its relationship with career counseling services received will allow us to more deeply analyze the studied problem. In Ukrainian system of secondary education, the duties of a career counselor are not yet institutionalized. Furthermore, there are no training programs for specialists who would provide professional career guidance and counseling, working in the education system. It should be mentioned that the first steps in this direction are currently being taken. In particular, at the Borys Grinchenko Kyiv Metropolitan University, with the support of the National Education Agency of Finland, educational programs for the training of career counselors are being developed (CARE, 2023). But the lack of institutionalization does not mean that Ukrainian high school seniors are deprived of the opportunity to receive assistance in choosing a future career. Currently, a wide range of career counseling functions are shared between school psychologists and high school teachers. Although this approach can only partially cover the functionality of trained career counselors, before introducing specialised career guidance and counseling into Ukrainian schools, it is important to understand what is already being implemented in this field and how it actually works.

documents.abstract: The proposed research project aims to advance the understanding of within-work recovery, focusing on the restorative effects of microbreaks that align with employees' psychological needs. Effective work recovery is crucial for occupational health and employee well-being, preventing burnout, reducing stress, and enhancing productivity. While after-work recovery is essential, within-work recovery, such as taking microbreaks, is equally important. Microbreaks, brief and informal breaks taken during the workday, have been shown to effectively restore employees' resources. Previous studies have explored various activities for microbreaks, yet these investigations often lack a solid theoretical foundation and fail to consider the employees' perspectives and needs. The primary aim of this study is to develop and validate the Person-Break Fit Theory and verify whether the effectiveness of microbreaks is moderated by the fit between the break activity and the employee's psychological needs. The study will employ a laboratory experiment involving 312 workers. Participants will undergo psychological needs assessments and repeated measurements of their energy resources before and after completing an exhausting office task, as well as after taking a microbreak. The experiment will feature three conditions: no break, a break that fits the participant's needs, and a break that does not fit their needs. The content of the microbreak will involve consuming short social media videos generated algorithmically. By investigating the interplay between microbreak activities and psychological needs, this study will contribute to the development of the Person-Break Fit Theory and provide empirically-validated recommendations for improving the quality of work breaks. This research will offer practical insights for enhancing employee well-being and productivity through optimized within-work recovery strategies.

Research has shown that curiosity plays a crucial role in human performance and well-being. Based on multi-dimensional models of curiosity, we examined potential underlying mechanisms for this relationship. Extending prior research, we expected state and trait variants of curiosity to predict more challenge and less threat appraisals for novel tasks (i.e., joyous exploration dimension), stronger dissatisfaction when denied opportunities to do something interesting (i.e., deprivation sensitivity dimension), and persist longer under stress states (i.e., stress tolerance). We asked 123 participants to prepare and deliver a speech titled "Why are you a good friend?" After preparation, participants were informed that they were randomly selected not to perform the task. Throughout the experiment, we recorded heart rate reactivity as a physiological indicator of task engagement. We found that individuals curious about the upcoming task felt more challenged, less threatened, and presented longer physiological engagement than less curious individuals. Curious individuals expressed more disappointment about the missed opportunity to deliver the speech. In summary, this study revealed theoretically derived mechanisms that partially account for associations between curiosity and positive life outcomes while also indicating adverse effects.

documents.abstract: Considering the escalation of multiple environmental crises, there is an increased need to understand the role of employees as active agents in the pursuit of organizational environmental sustainability. In this study, we develop and test a dynamic model of reciprocal relations between green work characteristics and proactive employee green behaviour (EGB). Drawing from action regulation theory, we examine how green job demands, autonomy, as well as supervisor and co-worker support contribute to co-worker-directed and organization-directed EGB, and vice versa. We adopted a four-wave longitudinal research design and collected monthly data from N = 1,887 employees in Germany. Results of a random intercept cross-lagged panel model showed that green job autonomy was positively related to subsequent co-worker-directed EGB. Furthermore, co-worker-directed EGB was positively related to subsequent green co-worker support and organization-directed EGB was positively related to subsequent green job demands. We also found evidence for positive behavioural spillover, suggesting that co-worker-directed EGB might subsequently motivate employees to engage in organization-directed EGB. In addition to advancing the understanding of the top-down work design processes that organizations can use to promote proactive EGB, the findings of this study provide insights into how employees can contribute bottom-up to greening work environments.

documents.abstract: As user centred design methods become more important for inclusive design, designers increasingly use methods borrowed from other disciplines such as Ethnography to gain insights into user behaviour. But what are the advantages in using ethnography to understand ergonomic requirements? And what form of insights does it result in? This paper offers findings and reflections from a design ethnographic case study of older people. It found that advantages in using ethnography lies in the depth and breadth of findings, resulting in a broad range of ergonomic and usability insights, and a deep understanding of lead users.

documents.abstract: Delirium is a frequently reported significant complication in acute and critically ill patients. Multimodal interventions can potentially decrease delirium incidence and severity by reducing predisposing factors. Previous research has documented the efficacy of delirium assessment and management interventions. However, the heterogeneity and complexity of these multimodal interventions make them challenging to disseminate and integrate into clinical practice. To support nurses in decision-making for delirium care, a clinical decision support system (CDSS) can increase situational awareness by reducing the cognitive load and facilitating relevant clinical information gathering. It can have a positive impact on nursing efficacy as well as on patient outcomes. This scoping review aims to map the existing literature on the use of CDSS to deliver multimodal interventions in delirium care for ICU adults, explore how it has been applied in this context, and identify gaps in the existing literature.

documents.abstract: Comprehensive overview of the Kalashnikov AK family of armament guns, detailing its historical significance, evolution, design features, global impact, and comparative analysis with contemporary firearms. It delves into the motivations behind the creation of the AK series, its various generations, and key variants, as well as its global proliferation and influence on modern combat. The document also highlights the design features that contribute to the AK family's reliability and durability, its user-friendly ergonomics, and its comparative analysis with the American M16 rifle. It concludes by emphasizing the AK family's enduring legacy as a hallmark of firearm design, widely respected for its performance, reliability, and versatility.

This multi-phase research project explores the decision-making processes of fire partners and publics in relation to National Weather Service (NWS) fire weather products, such as Fire Weather Watches (FWW) and Red Flag Warnings (RFW). These critical products are designed to alert fire management personnel and the public to impending fire weather conditions, but there is limited research on how they are utilized in practice. Through a collaborative, phased approach, my goal is to enhance the effectiveness of fire weather communication and inform intentional product improvements based on end-user operational needs. ________________________________________ Phase 1: Focus Groups with Fire Partners (Completed): In the first phase, I conducted 19 focus groups with 85 fire management partners across all six NWS regions. These discussions aimed to understand how fire partners interpret and use fire weather information from the NWS and other sources when making operational decisions leading up to wildfires. My findings revealed that while Red Flag Warnings (RFWs) were not a primary influence on operational decisions—since many participants were already aware of impending fire weather conditions—they were still valuable for public communication, justifying resource allocation, enhancing situational awareness (especially for less experienced personnel), and reinforcing confidence in prior decisions. The insights from this phase helped shape the initial recommendations for improving NWS fire weather products. These recommendations focus on targeted enhancements, rather than a complete overhaul, to better meet the evolving needs of fire management. For more detailed findings, you can access the AMS presentation summarizing elements from Phase 1: https://www.google.com/url?q=https://ams.confex.com/ams/105ANNUAL/meetingapp.cgi/Session/69350&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1744836859466146&usg=AOvVaw3q0kPA07FlqqCCjMOGmaFb. My talk begins at around 32 minutes; please note this recording is not available to the community (non-AMS members) until late April. ________________________________________ Phase 2: Surveys with Fire Partners (In Progress): Building on the insights from the focus groups, I am currently conducting surveys with fire partners to further explore how they use fire weather information from the NWS and other sources. This phase focuses on understanding the specific tools that fire partners find most valuable and how various information sources influence their operational decision making. They survey will also focus on their preferences and understanding of probabilistic fire weather information. The survey results will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges and gaps in fire weather communication and will allow us to identify opportunities for improvement in the issuance and content of products like FWWs and RFWs. ________________________________________ Phase 3: Public Survey (Future Phase): The final phase of this research will involve conducting a survey of the public to round out our understanding of fire weather decision-making. While fire partners are the intended primary users of fire weather products, understanding the public’s perception and understanding of these products is equally important for effective communication during wildfire events. This phase will also help to assess whether public awareness aligns with fire partner needs and how NWS products could be better tailored to inform both professionals and the general public in high-risk wildfire situations. ________________________________________ Collaborations with Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs): Throughout all phases of the study, I am collaborating with local Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) to ensure that the insights gained from fire partners and the public are directly informing the development of improved fire weather products. As a result, WFOs are continuously updated with the latest research findings, ensuring that the study remains relevant to ongoing operational needs and provides actionable recommendations. ________________________________________ Conclusion and Moving Forward: The ultimate goal of this research is to foster a research-to-operations-to-research cycle that informs both the development of NWS fire weather products and their practical use in fire management. By connecting research insights to operational decisions and continuously refining the products based on user feedback, this study aims to improve wildfire preparedness and response. As I move into the next phases of the study, I will continue to provide updates here, highlighting new findings and the next steps in our collaboration with fire partners and public stakeholders. The DesignSafe citation for the instruments used in this research and data collected can be found via: Hoekstra, S., 2025: Focus group/survey instruments. Evaluating National Weather Service Fire Weather Products within a Fire Partner and Public Decision-Making Context. DesignSafe-CI, https://doi.org/10.17603/ds2-89h2-de64.
